claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by formation and stabilization of a dynamic, self-renewing surface passivation or tribofilm.
The surface film repairs damage caused by mechanical wear.
A dense passivation film limits chemical attack.
An AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA with Mo addition can provide the proposed initial material state.
The proposed alloy has a multiphase microstructure containing elements predisposed to rapid passivation.
The hypothesis can be tested by sliding the alloy in 3.5% NaCl while varying contact pressure and sliding speed and monitoring electrochemical and surface responses in situ.
Mechanical wear intermittently removes the protective film.
Passivating alloy elements enable rapid re-passivation after film removal.
The balance between film removal and film reformation reduces wear-induced degradation.
The balance between film removal and film reformation reduces corrosion attack.
At moderate wear conditions, the dynamically passivating alloy will exhibit a lower wear rate than a baseline lacking effective dynamic passivation.
At moderate wear conditions, the dynamically passivating alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current than a baseline lacking effective dynamic passivation.
Excessive mechanical stress can prevent effective tribofilm reformation and increase combined degradation.
An overly aggressive corrosive medium can overwhelm re-passivation and increase combined degradation.
The prediction should hold when mechanical stress is moderate enough to permit timely tribofilm reformation.
Static corrosion tests without sliding or an alloy formulation lacking effective re-passivation can serve as the baseline.
Tribofilm thickness and stability, impedance, wear-related material loss, and corrosion current density are measurable observables for testing the hypothesis.
The hypothesis is falsified if tribofilm presence or stability is uncorrelated with wear and corrosion resistance, or if film formation produces no measurable improvement over the baseline.
